PCI.BIO: Dr. Lisa Longoria is a physician assistant and physician assistant educator from Edinburg, Texas. She is a Clinical Associate Professor in the Physician Assistant Department at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley and specializes in Family and Internal Medicine. She holds Bachelor's degrees in Music and PA studies (UTPA), Master's degrees in Music, PA Studies, and Counseling and Guidance (Texas A&M Kingsville and UTPA), and a Ph.D. in Leadership Studies from Our Lady of the Lake University. Dr. Longoria is a member of TAPA, AAPA, and PAEA. She is active in her department as the Primary Care Coordinator, Family Medicine faculty instructor, and serves on several departmental committees and college committees.
PCI.SKILLS: Areas of expertise: Internal Medicine, Family Practice

CONGRANT.SPONORG: Langston University, Langston's Rehabilitation Research and Training Center on Research (RRTC) and Capacity Building for Minority Entities, Oklahoma City, OK
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
In this study we hope to identify the perceptions of obesity, diet and exercise that Hispanic young adults with disabilities have. We will analyze
sample responses on their feelings about obesity and how they feel impacts their life as well as what challenges or barriers they face as they
try to live and active and healthy life and if they are even trying. The ultimate goal is that with the gained insight we can tailor interventions for
Hispanics with disabilities.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: The Relationship Between Physician Assistant Self-Efficacy and Leadership Style

INTELLCONT_AUTH.INSTITUTION: Our Lady of the Lake University
Our Lady of the Lake University
Our Lady of the Lake University

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
Abstract

The current study explored the relationship between physician assistants’ self-efficacy and leadership style. Participants included a total of 163 physician assistants in the United States. Self-efficacy was reported using the General Self-Efficacy Questionnaire (GSE) by Schwarzer and Jerusalem and leadership style was evaluated using the Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire (MLQ-5X) by Bass and Avolio. Autonomy was measured using the Independent Practice and Support Subscale of the Nurse Practitioner Primary Care Organizational Climate Questionnaire (NP-PCOCQ) by Poghosyan et al. A demographic survey included items relating to gender, age, ethnicity, and years of experience. After controlling for the demographic variables, multiple regression results indicated that self-efficacy significantly predicted leadership behaviors in physician assistants. Positive relationships were found between leader self-efficacy and self-reported transformational leadership (explained 21.2% of the variance) and transactional leadership (explained 12.2% of the variance). The results suggest that physician assistants with the self-regulation of thought processes, motivation, and self-confidence may engage in increased transformational and transactional leadership behaviors. These findings may inform leadership development among physician assistants by focusing on building self-efficacy in physician assistant students and practitioners.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: The Relationship between Physician Assistant Self-Efficacy and Leadership Style
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: The purpose of this study is to contribute to the body of knowledge in the area of physician assistants and leadership style. The study will examine the relationship between PA's self-efficacy and their leadership style. Results of the Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire (MLQ) encompassing the Full Range Model of Leadership (Transformational, Transactional, Passive Avoidant) will be assessed. Self-efficacy will be measured with the General Self-Efficacy Scale (GSE).

PRESENT.NAME: PAEA Forum 2021
PRESENT.TITLE: The Relationship Between Physician Assistant Self-Efficacy and Leadership Style
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: By considering physician assistants’ self-efficacy and leadership style, this study examines whether self-confidence plays a role in physician assistants’ performance of tasks and responsibilities or whether Self-efficacy determines Leadership behaviors (Transformational, Transactional, and Passive Avoidant Leadership). In addition, age, gender, ethnicity, years of practice experience, and autonomy will determine any impact on leadership behavior. For this study, a convenience sample of 2,608 practicing physician assistants from the Texas Academy of Physician Assistants, Rio Grande Valley PA Society, Bexar County PA Society and the Texas Pediatric Physician Assistant Society were asked to complete a 4-item demographic survey, the 36-item Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire, the 9-item General Self-Efficacy Scale, and a 10-item Autonomy scale. Participants included a total of 163 practicing PAs in the United States.The research design included a non-experimental design in this study in order to collect and analyze data determining the relationship between Self-Efficacy and Leadership style. The relationship was measured by a demographic survey and three survey instruments. The demographic survey included items relating to gender, age, ethnicity, and years of experience. The Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire (MLQ) evaluated the self-reported leadership behaviors of physician assistants, the General Self-Efficacy Scale (GSE) evaluated the self-rated self-efficacy of physician assistants, and the Independent Practice and Support Subscale was used to evaluate physician assistants’ self-reported autonomy. In this non-experimental research study, descriptive statistics were used for Self-Efficacy, the dimensions of Transformational, Transactional, and Passive Avoidant Leadership, including their respective facets, and control variables encompassing gender, age, ethnicity, years of experience, and autonomy. All continuous variables were analyzed with Pearson r correlations and the statistical analysis of this study included multiple regression. Confidence levels were established at 95% (p < .05).
